claims.claim: Pleasure in articulate sound and its symbolic use is independent of communication though entangled with it, and must never be forgotten in language-making.
An invented language with individual flavour must have a mythology woven into it, and conversely language construction will breed a mythology — names and tongue come first, the world grows to fit.
claims.quote: your language construction will breed a mythology

claims.claim: Tolkien's chief interest is word-form in itself and word-form in relation to meaning, the so-called phonetic fitness.

claims.feature: verse as the test of an invented language
claims.claim: The final fruition of an invented language is verse, which both expresses and fixes the maker's personal taste in sound.
In modern poetry word-form is seldom consciously marked and its effects are miscalled 'authentic magic'; Tolkien wants sound-pattern deliberately constructed to give pleasure.
claims.quote: the word-form is seldom consciously marked

claims.claim: Word-form even unassociated with notions can give a perception of beauty; Greek, Finnish and Welsh are named as languages with characteristically beautiful word-form.
claims.quote: capable of giving pleasure - a perception of beauty

claims.feature: association of form and sense (cellar door)
claims.claim: 'Cellar door' is beautiful dissociated from its sense, and the higher pleasure lies in words where form and sense associate — a phonaesthetic test the prose can be held to.
claims.quote: the association of form and sense

claims.claim: Linguistic taste is partly inborn (the 'native tongue' as distinct from the cradle-tongue), so a writer's phonaesthetic choices express inherent predilections rather than fashion.
claims.source: Anna Smol, 'Tolkien's cellar door' (quoting 'English and Welsh' pp.190-1)

claims.feature: illusion of historical truth and perspective
claims.claim: The illusion of historical truth and perspective in Beowulf is largely a product of art — an instinctive historical sense used with a poetical, not historical, object.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics' (full text PDF)

claims.claim: The impression of depth is the effect and justification of episodes and allusions to old tales that are darker and more desperate than the foreground — the background must be grimmer than the story.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: mostly darker, more pagan, and desperate than the foreground

claims.claim: Old stones (sources) exist to build the tower from whose top one sees the sea; the work is art, not a quarry, and its sources must not be dug for at the tower's expense.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'

claims.claim: The poem's structure is a balance, an opposition of ends and beginnings (youth against age), not a steadily advancing narrative.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'
claims.quote: an opposition of ends and beginnings

claims.claim: Old English lines are founded on a balance of two opposed halves, more like masonry than music, and the whole is a composition not a tune.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'

claims.claim: Beowulf is not an epic but an heroic-elegiac poem whose first 3,136 lines are the prelude to a dirge — the elegiac is the governing tone.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'

claims.feature: late, antiquarian voice (echo of an echo)
claims.claim: The poem is late not primitive: its maker told of things already old and weighted with regret, producing sorrows both poignant and remote.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'Beowulf: The Monsters and the Critics'

verdicts.trueWording: pleasure in articulate sound... must not be forgotten for a moment
verdicts.note: Raw PDF (gwern, 26pp, pypdf text). Quote 'pleasure in articulate sound' appears once, verbatim: 'the more individual and personal factor - pleasure in articulate sound, and in the symbolic use of it, independent of communication though constantly in fact entangled with it - must not be forgotten for a moment.' Every limb (independent of communication; entangled with it; must not be forgotten) is on the page. 'in language-making' is context-supported: the sentence sits in the essay on invented languages and the next sentence applies it to Naffarin, his own construction.

verdicts.trueWording: your language construction will breed a mythology
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Limbs 1-2 fully supported: 'to give your language an individual flavour, it must have woven into it the threads of an individual mythology' and 'The converse indeed is true, your language construction will breed a mythology.' The third limb is not on this page: 'A Secret Vice' nowhere says names come first or that a world grows to fit them. Greps for names/world/stories return only unrelated passages (Animalic animal names, Welsh names on coal-trucks, 'history of the world'). The names-first/world-to-fit formulation is Letters #165/#180, not this essay. Language->mythology priority IS supported; names and world are not.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: names and tongue come first, the world grows to fit

verdicts.trueWording: I am personally most interested perhaps in word-form in itself
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'I am personally most interested perhaps in word-form in itself, and in word-form in relation to meaning (so-called phonetic fitness) than in any other department.' 'Chief interest' is carried by 'than in any other department'; 'so-called phonetic fitness' is verbatim and parenthetical exactly as claimed.

verdicts.trueWording: this final fruition: verse... expresses, and has fixed, my personal taste
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: '...has had a long enough history of development to allow of this final fruition: verse. It expresses, and at the same time has fixed, my personal taste.' 'Taste in sound' is supported by the same sentence's opening: the language was 'expressly designed to give play to my own most normal phonetic taste'.

verdicts.trueWording: we call it the 'authentic magic' of the poet, meaningless expression
verdicts.note: Both halves verbatim on the page. Quote: 'the use of significant language is so habitual that the word-form is seldom consciously marked' — and it is explicitly 'poetry (of our day)'. The 'authentic magic' limb: 'we pause to wonder why a line or couplet produces an effect beyond its significance; we call it the authentic magic of the poet, or some such meaningless expression' — 'meaningless expression' supports 'miscalled'. Deliberate construction limb: 'this construction of sounds to give pleasure', which such inventions 'sharpen... by making them more conscious'.

verdicts.trueWording: Greek, Finnish, Welsh... capable of producing this pleasure
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'The very word-form itself, of course, even unassociated with notions, is capable of giving pleasure - a perception of beauty...' followed immediately by 'Greek, Finnish, Welsh (to name at random languages which have a very characteristic and in their different ways beautiful wordform, readily seizable by the sensitive at first sight) are capable of producing this pleasure.' All three languages named, in that order, as characteristically beautiful in word-form.

verdicts.trueWording: pleasure in the contemplation of the association of form and sense
verdicts.note: Live URL returned HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and a browser-UA curl; recovered via Wayback raw capture (web.archive.org/web/20260306100734id_/...), so this is the raw page, not a summary. Quote verbatim. Limb 1 verbatim: 'cellar door is beautiful, especially if dissociated from its sense (and from its spelling)'. Limb 2 verbatim: 'moving to the higher dimension, the words in which there is pleasure in the contemplation of the association of form and sense are abundant.' Attribution to the 1955 lecture 'English and Welsh' is stated on the page. The trailing clause 'a phonaesthetic test the prose can be held to' is the sweep's own application, not an assertion about the source.

Quote 'inherent linguistic predilections' is verbatim, with the claimed p.190 citation, and the page supplies the p.191 cellar-door passage — so the pp.190-1 source line is right. But the page never mentions a native tongue or a cradle-tongue: greps for 'cradle', 'native tongue' and bare 'native' return zero hits, and 'fashion' returns zero. The page's support for inbornness is only 'inherent linguistic predilections' plus 'everyone has a preference for certain sounds dissociated from the meanings of words'. The native/cradle-tongue distinction is genuinely in 'English and Welsh', but it is NOT on this cited page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the 'native tongue' as distinct from the cradle-tongue (and 'rather than fashion')

verdicts.trueWording: illusion of historical truth... largely a product of art
verdicts.note: Raw PDF (22pp, pypdf). Quote verbatim: 'The illusion of historical truth and perspective, that has made Beowulf seem such an attractive quarry, is largely a product of art.' Next sentence carries the rest: 'The author has used an instinctive historical sense... but he has used it with a poetical and not an historical object.'

verdicts.trueWording: impression of depth... episodes and allusions, mostly darker than the foreground
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'This impression of depth is an effect and a justification of the use of episodes and allusions to old tales, mostly darker, more pagan, and desperate than the foreground.' Effect-and-justification and darker-than-foreground limbs both verbatim. The closing gloss 'the background must be grimmer than the story' is a normative restatement of the same sentence, and Tolkien's own 'effect and a justification' framing licenses it.

verdicts.trueWording: from that tower's top he could look out upon the sea
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, and the whole allegory is on the page: 'A man inherited a field in which was an accumulation of old stone, part of an older hall... Of the rest he took some and built a tower... So they pushed the tower over' to look for carvings, another 'began to dig' for coal 'and forgot even the stones' — 'But from the top of that tower the man had been able to look out upon the sea.' The art-not-quarry limb is verbatim elsewhere: 'Beowulf has been used as a quarry of fact and fancy far more assiduously than it has been studied as a work of art.'

verdicts.trueWording: essentially a balance, an opposition of ends and beginnings
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim: 'But the poem was not meant to advance, steadily or unsteadily. It is essentially a balance, an opposition of ends and beginnings.' Youth-against-age limb verbatim in the next sentence: 'an elaboration of the ancient and intensely moving contrast between youth and age, first achievement and final death.' Not-a-narrative limb: 'we must dismiss... the notion that Beowulf is a narrative poem'.

verdicts.trueWording: more like masonry than music; a composition not a tune
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim. Full support: 'The lines do not go according to a tune. They are founded on a balance; an opposition between two halves of roughly equivalent phonetic weight, and significant content... They are more like masonry than music.' The whole-is-a-composition limb is verbatim on the page too, applied to the poem's total structure: 'It is a composition not a tune.'

verdicts.trueWording: an heroic-elegiac poem; first 3,136 lines the prelude to a dirge
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, with every limb: 'Beowulf is not an epic, not even a magnified lay... if we must have a term, we should choose rather elegy. It is an heroic-elegiac poem; and in a sense all its first 3,136 lines are the prelude to a dirge'. The 3,136 figure matches exactly, and 'we should choose rather elegy' supports the elegiac as governing tone.

verdicts.trueWording: not a 'primitive' poem; it is a late one
verdicts.note: Quote 'an echo of an echo' verbatim. Late-not-primitive limb verbatim on p.15: 'Beowulf is not a primitive poem; it is a late one, using the materials (then still plentiful) preserved from a day already changing and passing'. Remaining limbs verbatim: 'its maker was telling of things already old and weighted with regret, and he expended his art in making keen that touch upon the heart which sorrows have that are both poignant and remote... it is to us as a memory brought over the hills, an echo of an echo.'
